Surah al-Qalam

It is among the first portions of the Qur'an to be revealed at Makkah. According to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, it was revealed after ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], then this surah, then al-Muzzammil, then al-Muddaththir. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), it is stated that it is Makkan without disagreement among the commentators. In al-Itqan (by al-Suyuti), it is stated that an exception is made from it: ﴿Indeed, We have tried them﴾ up to ﴿they used to say﴾ [al-Qalam: 17-33], and from ﴿So be patient﴾ up to ﴿the righteous﴾ [al-Qalam: 48-50], which is Madani; this was related by al-Sakhawi.

In Jamal al-Qurra', its verses are fifty-two by consensus. Its connection to Surah al-Mulk is, as it is said, that the one ends with a warning and this one begins with it. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said concerning this: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned at the end of al-Mulk the threat of making the water sink into the earth, He then emphasized in this surah the destruction of the fruit of the owners of the garden by a visitation during a night, which went round them while they were sleeping, so that they woke in the morning and found no trace of it, until they thought they had lost their way. If this happened to the fruit, which are dense bodies, then water, which is subtle, is closer to being removed; for this reason He, glorified is He, said here ﴿while they were sleeping﴾ and ﴿so it became like the reaped field﴾ [al-Qalam: 19, 20], and He, exalted is He, said there ﴿If your water should become sunk into the earth﴾ [al-Mulk: 30], as an indication that it will be taken away in a night, just as the fruit was taken away in a night. End of quotation. It is not without beauty.

Abu Hayyan said concerning it: He mentioned earlier things about the conditions of the blessed and the wretched, and mentioned His overpowering power and His vast knowledge, and that, were He to will, He, mighty and majestic, could cause the earth to swallow them or send upon them a violent wind; and what He, glorified is He, informed of is what was revealed to His Messenger ﷺ, and he recited it to them, peace and blessings be upon him. The disbelievers used to attribute it, at one time to poetry, at another to magic, and at another to madness. So He, majestic is His glory, began this noble surah by clearing His Messenger ﷺ of what they attributed to him of madness, and by magnifying his reward for his patience with their harm, and by praising his character. So He, mighty and majestic, said: ( In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful ). The nun is pronounced with sukun due to pause (waqf). Most readers read the nun with sukun and assimilate it into the waw of ﴿wal-qalam﴾, with ghunnah according to some and without it according to others. It is also read with a kasrah.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa, in one report from him, read it with a fathah, and both are because of the meeting of two sakin letters. It is permitted that the fathah be due to an elided particle of oath in the genitive position, like the saying "Allahi la-af'alanna" with the genitive; and that it be in the accusative by an elided verb such as "adhkur" or the like, not as a fathah of indeclinability. The non-declension is due to definiteness and femininity, on the basis that it is a proper name for the surah. Then, if it is taken as a name for the letter, recited in the manner of enumeration for challenge, as is well known and explained in its place; or as a name for the surah, in the accusative in the manner mentioned, or in the nominative on the basis that it is the predicate of an elided subject. They said: in His saying ﴿wal-qalam﴾ the waw is for oath; and if the thing sworn by is taken to be the qalam, then the waw is for conjunction with the preceding (nun), according to the prevalent view. The early scholars (salaf) chose that nun is among the mutashabih (ambiguous) letters, and many of the later scholars (khalaf) held that here it is among the names of the letters.

They said: What supports this is that if it were a common noun or a proper name, it would be declined with tanwin or be prevented from declension, and it would be written as it is pronounced. That its writing is as you see, for the intention of pausing and treating connection as pause, is contrary to the original; and that the script of the Mushaf is not subject to analogy is accepted, but the original is that it be treated according to analogy as far as possible. It is also said that it is the name of a fish upon which the earth rests, called al-Yahmut, with a fathah on the ya' with two dots below and a sukun on the ha'. In a hadith related by al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah and al-Hakim, who authenticated it...

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Allah, exalted is He, created the nun, and the earth was spread upon it; the nun moved, and the earth shook, so it was made firm with mountains. Then he recited ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ etc. This was related from Mujahid, and it was also related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak that it is the name of the inkwell (dawah). Al-Zamakhshari denied that the word nun occurs with the meaning of inkwell in the language or in established usage. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be a dialectal usage of some Arabs, or an Arabic-form foreign word, and he recited the verse of the poet:

When longing for them overwhelmed me, the nun cast down tears flowing abundantly.

Among the first commentators, some explained the qalam as that which wrote on the Preserved Tablet what will be until the Day of Resurrection; others explained it as the pen of the noble recording angels. The alif-lam in it, on both explanations, is for previous reference (ahd). Others explained it by genus, with the definite article being generic. Some, a few, explained it by what has preceded as well; but the apparent meaning of their words is that the inkwell is not the well-known inkwell, but an inkwell created on the day that pen was created.

It is related from Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, raising it to the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, nun is a tablet of light, and the qalam is a pen of light, running with what will be until the Day of Resurrection."

It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that it is a river of the rivers of Paradise. In al-Bahr: perhaps none of that is authentic, meaning none of all that has been mentioned about nun, except its being a name of letters. Apparently, if he was acquainted with the reports we have mentioned, he did not consider the authentication of al-Hakim concerning what was first related from Ibn 'Abbas, nor that one of its transmitters is al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, which in terms of evaluation is a corroboration of the sahih collections, nor the multitude of those who related from him; and this is what prevails in opinion, because of the great divergence in what is related from him concerning the intended meaning of it, to the extent that it is related from him that it is the last letter of the Name al-Rahman, and that this majestic Name was divided among ra, ha, and nun. It is not hidden that if the fish or a river in Paradise is intended, the speech becomes of the type of "How many a caliph, and a thousand eggplants." As for if the inkwell is intended, the indefiniteness rejects that most strongly; moreover, as you have heard from al-Zamakhshari, it is a language that has not been established, and the refutation of it can only be accomplished by establishing that from trustworthy authorities.

(And how...) with it. Mentioning the author of al-Qamus does not suffice as proof that it is a lexical meaning. The validity of the reports is open to discussion. The verse which Ibn 'Atiyyah recited has not been established as Arabic. As for its meaning the fish, applied to the inkwell figuratively by the relation of resemblance, since some fish yield a substance blacker than soot with which one writes—this is not hidden in its crudeness, for that kind has not become so well known that it can be made the thing compared; besides, the denier has no indication of that specific kind. As for its meaning the letter, figuratively for it, it is even more severe and bitter. So it is said; and there is room for discussion regarding "some." For storytellers, this section contains reports which are not relied upon and should not be listened to. Then, that the pen deserves magnification through swearing by it, when what is meant is the pen of the Preserved Tablet, which the reports say was the first thing Allah, exalted is He, created, or the pen of the noble recording angels, is evident.

As for the deserving of what is in people's hands, if the genus is meant, it is because of the abundance of its benefits; and even if it had no excellence other than being the instrument for writing down the books of Allah, mighty and majestic, that alone would be sufficient virtue to make it worthy of honor. As for the pronoun in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and what they inscribe﴾, i.e., what they write: either it refers to the pen, meaning the pen of the Preserved Tablet, and He expressed it with a plural pronoun to magnify it; or it refers to the pen meaning the genus of that with which writing is done, so the plural pronoun is for its multiplicity; yet it is not truly a writer, but rather an instrument for the writer, so the attribution to it is an attribution to an instrument figuratively. The expression for it with the pronoun of rational beings is because it stands in their place and is made the agent; or it refers to the scribes or the guardians, both understood from the pen, the first of them, by considering that the pen's owners are meant by the pen, figuratively, or by assuming a governed noun with it. What is most suitable of these is not hidden. As for it being for "ma" (what), which is in the sense of "man" (who), that is cold artifice. The apparent meaning in it is that it is either a relative pronoun, i.e., "and that which they inscribe," or a verbal noun, i.e., "and their inscribing."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 2:**

﴿Ma anta bi-ni'mati rabbika bi-majnun﴾ (You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman). This is the response to the oath. The second bāʾ (bāʾ) is extra (*ziyāda*), for the emphasis of negation. *Majnūn* (mad, possessed) is the predicate of *mā* (the negating particle). The first bāʾ indicates accompaniment (*mulābasa*, being joined to something) and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a clause describing the state of the subject). The governing word is *majnūn*, and its bāʾ does not prevent it from governing, because it is extra.

Nasir al-Din criticised this, saying that there is a problem in its meaning. He justified it by saying that its sense, on this reading, is that madness was negated from you at the time you were joined to the favour of your Lord, and it is not understood from this that madness in general was negated from him, may prayers and peace be upon him. And what else is meant but this?

It was said in response to this: it is not hidden that this objection applies to the reading he himself preferred. That is because the meaning then becomes: madness was negated from you while you were joined to the favour of your Lord, and it is not understood from this that it was negated from him, peace be upon him, at all times, which is what is meant.

It was answered that this state is necessarily attached to him, may prayers and peace be upon him, and is never separated from him, so negating it in that state entails negating it from him always and in all other states. It was objected that this holds under both readings and is not specific to one of them rather than the other. But you should know that he distinguished between them, since on the reading where the governing word is *majnūn*, as has been indicated, the meaning becomes: madness that befell you during the aforementioned state of joining was negated from you. This indicates the possibility of its occurring in that state, indeed its actual occurrence, and that is a vain meaning, for how can madness be conceived as existing and occurring at the time he was joined to the favour, and among that favour is soundness of mind (*ḥaṣāfa*)? This objection does not apply to the preferred reading, since the negation understood then is not directed at madness qualified by what was mentioned. And although it is qualified in it too, there is no harm in this, because its qualifier is necessarily inherent in the essence of what is negated, as you have understood.

It was also said: if the bāʾ is taken to indicate causation and the adverbial phrase is taken as unattached (*laghw*), it becomes clear that it is not permissible to attach it to what follows in meaning, as in the verse:

*ẓuhūru nāri al-qirā laylan ʿalā ʿilmin*
(the kindling of the fire of hospitality at night is known)

Al-Khafaji mentioned a discussion concerning the circumstantial clause and the circumstance when they occur after a negation, and he verified that in that case what is necessary is only the negation of the circumstance's coinciding with the one it describes, not the negation of the circumstance itself. So reflect on this and do not be heedless.

He (al-Alusi, citing another) permitted that ﴿bi-ni'mati rabbika﴾ be an intervening oath within the speech, for its emphasis, without assuming a response, or that a response be assumed which is indicated by the preceding speech. Abu Hayyan favoured this second view. The mention of the attribute of lordship (*rubūbiyya*), which indicates elevation to the heights of perfection, together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, is for his honour, and as a notification that He, exalted is He, completes His favour upon him and raises him in exaltedness to a limit beyond which there is no limit. The purpose is to exonerate him, peace be upon him, from what they used to ascribe to him of madness, out of envy, enmity and obstinacy. So the sum of the statement is: you are free from what they say.

**﴿And indeed for you﴾**, in return for your enduring the various hardships from them and your bearing the burdens of the Message, **﴿a reward﴾**, a great reward whose measure cannot be estimated, **﴿unending﴾**, i.e., uncut off, despite its greatness. Or [it means] **unending for you** on the part of people, for it is His bounty, exalted be He, without intermediary. Or [it means] on His part, exalted be He, because you are the beloved of God, exalted be He, and He, mighty and majestic, is the Most Generous of the generous. It is among the characteristics of the generous that they do not reproach others for their benefactions, especially when the benefaction is toward their beloved, as the poet said:

*I will thank a lifespan, if my death is delayed, for favours that were not bestowed with reproach, though they were great.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 4:

﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ No one among the creation can attain its far reach (sha'w), and for this reason he endures from them what those of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm) among your peers could not endure.

In the hadith related by Muslim, Abu Dawud, Imam Ahmad, al-Darimi, Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Sa'd ibn Hisham, who said: "I said to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: 'O Mother of the Believers, inform me about the character (khuluq) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' She said: 'Do you not recite the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed, the character of the Prophet of Allah was the Qur'an.'"

She meant by this, as has been said, that all the noble qualities that are in it (the Qur'an) were present in him ﷺ, and that what it contains of restraint from base character (safsaf al-akhlaq) was something by which he ﷺ was restrained, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the primary addressee of the address. ﴿Thus (We revealed it) that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. Perhaps her saying points back to this, as in the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir and others, on the authority of Abu al-Darda', that he asked her about his character, peace and blessings be upon him, and she said: "His character was the Qur'an: he is pleased with what pleases it and angered by what angers it."

Al-'Arif bi-Allah al-Marsafi said: She meant by her saying "his character was the Qur'an" that he took on the attributes of Allah the Exalted, but she did not state it explicitly, out of courtesy. In al-Kashf it is said that there is embedded in this sentence that he ﷺ is characterized by the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, through His saying, glorified is He, ﴿tremendous﴾. Some have claimed that in the verse there is an allusion that good character is something that does not combine with madness, and that the more a person's character is good, the further he is from madness, and it follows from this that bad character is close to madness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verses 5–6:

﴿So you will see and they will see﴾ ﴿which of you is the afflicted [maftun]﴾. That is, the madman (al-majnun), as related by Ibn Jarir from Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jubayr, and Abd ibn Humayd from Mujahid. The term was applied to the madman because he is afflicted (futina), that is, tested (muhhina) with madness. It was also said that the Arabs believed madness to be the result of the jinn's bewitchment, and that they are the ones who afflict (al-fattan) the one they afflict among them. Here the ba' is extra (mazidah) in the subject (mubtada'), which Sibawayh permitted. Or [maftun is] a verbal noun (masdar) meaning affliction (al-fitnah), so that al-maftun is a masdar like al-ma'qul and al-majlud, meaning madness, as related by Abd ibn Humayd from al-Hasan and Abu al-Jawza. This is based on the view that a masdar may come in the form of the passive participle (maf'ul), as some have permitted, and the ba' is then for accompaniment (al-mulabasah). Or the meaning is: which of the two groups among you is the madness, is it the group of believers or the group of disbelievers; that is, in which of them is found one who deserves this name. This is an allusion to Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their like.

On this view the ba' has the sense of fi (in), and one supposes "which of the two groups among you," to avoid the objection that the address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and a group of the Quraysh, and that one cannot say to a group and an individual "in which of you is Zayd." The objection is reinforced by the fact that the words "So you will see" are addressed to him ﷺ alone. The answer to this reinforcement is that the address, in its outward sense, is restricted to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that the speech follows the pattern of what precedes it and is not discordant; yet it is not truly restricted in the way of what precedes it, since the community (ummah) is also included in it, so the supposition "which of the two groups" is valid. The author of al-Kashf claimed that this is the best of the options, because it conveys allusion (ta'ridh) and avoids the use of rare usages: the extra ba' in the subject, and the verbal noun being in the form of the passive participle. This is the view of al-Farra', and the reading of Ibn Abi Abla, "ayyukum" (with the ending), supports it. Whatever the case, the apparent meaning is that ﴿which of you is the afflicted﴾ is governed by what precedes it by way of dispute (tanazu'), and the intended meaning is: "you will know" and "they will know" that on the Day of Resurrection, when the truth becomes distinct from falsehood. This was related from Ibn Abbas. It was also said that ﴿So you will see and they will see﴾ refers to this world, through the manifestation of the outcome of the matter, by the victory of Islam, your domination over them through killing and plunder, your becoming awe-inspiring and esteemed in the hearts of the worlds, and their becoming humiliated and debased. This includes what happened on the day of Badr.

It is related from Muqatil that this is a threat of the punishment of the day of Badr. Abu Uthman al-Mazini said: the speech is complete at His words ﴿and they will see﴾, and then He, glorified is He, resumes with ﴿which of you is the afflicted﴾ as an interrogative meaning that it is intended to present a choice between two matters, the negation of the judgment from one of them is known, and the determination of its existence for the other. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining what precedes it and emphasizing what it contains of promise and threat. That is, He, glorified is He, is ﴿most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾, the one who leads to the happiness of both abodes, and who wandered in the bewilderment of misguidance, heading toward what it requires of everlasting wretchedness and increased punishment. This is the madman who does not distinguish between benefit and harm, but thinks harm is benefit and so chooses it, and thinks benefit is harm and so abandons it. (And He) ﷿, is ﴿most knowing of those who are guided﴾ to His way, the ones who attain every desired thing and are saved from every feared thing, and they are the intelligent, the ones who prefer the better course. So He recompenses each of the two groups according to what it deserves of punishment and reward.

In al-Kashshaf (a Qur'anic commentary by al-Zamakhshari), it says: "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the madmen in the true sense, and they are those who have strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of the intelligent, and they are the guided." Or it may be a threat and a promise, and that He, glorified is He, is most knowing of the recompense of the two groups. In al-Kashf (a commentary on al-Kashshaf by al-Tibi), he said: "It is, on the first reading, a concluding emphatic statement (tadhyil) confirming what was alluded to earlier, that the afflicted one is the one who ascribed madness to you. It follows the method of emphasis without explicit statement, but in a clearer manner, for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿which of you is the afflicted one﴾ has no specification in any way, and this is an apposition: ﴿He is most knowing﴾ of the madman and of the sane person. It indicates that madness, in this sense, is not what they imagined, and it is established for them that misguidance is diverted in the very form of this claim. On the second reading, it is also a concluding statement, but in the manner of explicit statement, because ﴿those who have strayed﴾ stands in the place of (them), and ﴿those who are guided﴾ stands in the place of (you). What we have considered is perhaps the more beneficial. It seems that placing the threat first is so that it connects with what was indicated at the beginning, and the expression concerning straying is in the verbal form to indicate that it is contrary to what the natural disposition requires. And the addition of ﴿He is most knowing﴾ serves to increase the affirmation, along with the notice of the difference in recompense."

The fa' in His words ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ indicates that the prohibition follows from what precedes it, namely his (ﷺ) guidance and their misguidance. Alternatively, it follows from everything that was mentioned from the beginning of the surah. This is an incitement and a spurring on to persist in opposing them, meaning: continue in what you are upon, of not obeying them, and be steadfast in that. It is also permissible that it be a prohibition against flattering them and accommodating them by showing the opposite of what is in his (ﷺ) heart, in order to win their hearts, not a prohibition against actually obeying them. This is indicated by His words ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾, because it is a reason for the prohibition or for the cessation. He expressed it as "obedience" only for the sake of emphasis in warning against them. The meaning is: they love that you would soften toward them and be lenient with them in some matters, ﴿and they would compromise﴾, i.e., they would then compromise, or they are now compromising, hoping for your compromise. So the fa' is for causation, introducing a clause caused by what precedes it, and the subject has been omitted because the verb is in the indicative mood.

The difference between the two readings is that the meaning, if they wish that you would compromise so that their compromise follows yours, makes one compromise follow the other in reality, and in this case *law* (لَوْ) is not verbal (i.e., it is the conditional particle). According to the second reading, it is verbal (i.e., it introduces a clause meaning "that"), and the sequence is mental, following from their love and wish. It is also permissible that the fa' be a conjunction linking *yudhinūna* (they compromise) to *tudhinu* (you compromise), on the basis that it falls within the scope of *law* as something wished, similar to it. The meaning would then be: they love that they would compromise immediately after your compromise. What precedes is further from being subject to dispute and debate. Whichever of these is the case, what is considered on their side is the true meaning of *idhān* (compromise), which is displaying softness and concealing its opposite. As for his (peace be upon him) side, what is considered with respect to their love is only the display of softness, and the concealing of its opposite is not within consideration; rather, they are in the utmost hatred of it. Its consideration is only with respect to him (peace be upon him).

In some copies of the Qur'an, as Harun said, the reading is *fayudhinū* without the nun of the indicative ending. It was said that it is in the subjunctive mood, as the answer to the wish understood from *waddū* (they love). It was also said that it is a conjunction linking it to *tudhinu*, on the basis that *law* functions like the subjunctive *anna* (that), so it has no answer. From it and what follows it, a verbal noun is formed which serves as the object of *waddū*. It is as if it were said: they love that you would compromise, so that they would compromise. Perhaps this is what is meant by the one who said it is a conjunction on the assumption of *anna* (the implied subjunctive). Most grammarians hold that *law* retains its original meaning, and its answer is omitted. The object of *waddū* is likewise omitted, meaning: they love your compromise, if you would compromise, so that they would compromise; they would be delighted by that.

Among those who held that it occurs in this world is the one who said it is a threat concerning what befell him on the Day of Badr, for he was struck on it with a sword, and a mark remained on his snout. But what is well known in the books of biography and hadith is that Abu Jahl was killed on the Day of Badr, and the rest, other than al-Hakam, died before him, so none of them was branded with that mark. Likewise al-Hakam did not know that he had been branded with that, although he did not die before him.

From al-Nadr ibn Shumayl it is related that *al-khartum* means wine, and he recited:

*You spend your day in amusement and play, and at night you are a drinker of the *kharatim* (wine-cups).*

And the meaning would be: We shall impose the hadd (prescribed punishment) on him for drinking it. This is criticised on the grounds that the report negates it, since those disbelievers perished, other than al-Hakam, before the prohibition of wine, and it is not established that he was given the hadd. Moreover, they were not bound by the legal rulings. And it is also refuted by the difficulty of the wording and the loss of the grandeur of the meaning.

﴿Indeed, We tested them﴾: i.e., We struck the people of Makkah with a calamity, namely drought, through the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His saying was: "O Allah, press down Your hand upon Mudar and make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf."

﴿As We tested﴾: i.e., like what We tested. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position as an adjective of an understood verbal noun, and "ma" (ما) is a verbal particle (مصدرية). It was also said that "ma" means "alladhi" (الذي), so the meaning is "like the trial which We inflicted upon" ﴿the people of the garden﴾, the well-known garden whose produce was famous among them. It was in the land of Yemen, near Sana'a, belonging to a man who used to give Allah's due from it. When he died, it passed to his son, who prevented people from its produce and withheld Allah's due from it. So what Allah mentioned happened. It is related by Ibn al-Mundhir and others, from Ibn Jarir, that it was in a land in Yemen called Sawran, six miles from Sana'a.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas: they were people from Abyssinia. Their father had a garden, and he used to feed the poor from it. When he died, his sons said: "Our father was indeed foolish to feed the poor." So they swore that they would not feed a single poor person from it.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that he said: it belonged to an elderly man of the Children of Israel, who would keep the food for his year and give away the surplus in charity. His sons used to forbid him from giving charity. When he died, they swore to deny the poor.

In another narration, it belonged to a righteous man two farsakhs from Sana'a, and he would leave for the poor what the sickle missed, what was at the bottom of the heaps, what the picking of grapes missed, and what remained on the mat beneath the palm when it was cut. Much would thus accumulate for them. When he died, his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will become hard for us, and we are people with dependants." So they swore to harvest it early in the morning, secretly from the poor, as the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿When they swore﴾: this is a clause governed by "balawna" (بلونا). ﴿That they would surely harvest it﴾: that they would surely cut its fruit after it had ripened. ﴿In the morning﴾: entering the morning.

This is a report of their oath, not of its literal wording. Otherwise it would have said "lanasrumanna" (لنصرمنها) with the first-person plural nun (نون المتكلمين). Both forms are permissible in such a construction.

[p. 30]

﴿And they did not make an exception﴾. It was said: that is, they did not say, "If God wills." Calling it an exception (istithna') even though it is a conditional (shart) is because its effect is the same as that of an exception. Your saying "I will surely go out, if God wills" and "I will not go out except if God wills" have one meaning. The Imam said: the root of istithna' is from thanya, which means restraint and turning back, and by restricting the oath with a condition, one turns back its binding force. Therefore, applying the term to it is literal usage. It was also said: that is, they did not turn back from what they had resolved upon, namely withholding from the poor. On both views, the apparent reading is that it is coordinated with ﴿they swore﴾, so the expected wording would be "and they did not make an exception." It seems that he turned away from that wording to this one in order to bring the scene before the mind, because of what it contains of strangeness, since the fitting thing in an oath, given what it entails, is the abandonment of obedience. In al-Kashshaf it is said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "not making exceptions." The shift to the present tense (al-mudari') carries a kind of emphasis and an alert to the place of their error, and there is in it an allusion to what we have mentioned. It was also said: the meaning is "and they do not set aside the share of the poor, as their father used to give it." On this view, it is coordinated with the words of God, Exalted, ﴿they will surely harvest it﴾, and the thing sworn to; or it is coordinated with His words, glorified be He, ﴿at dawn﴾, which is a circumstantial clause. This meaning is free from any objection.

﴿فَطافَ عَلَيْها﴾ means it encompassed it, descending upon the garden. ﴿طائِفٌ﴾ means an all-encompassing affliction. It is thus an adjective of an omitted noun. Qatadah's view that ﴿طائِفٌ﴾ means a punishment explains the basic meaning, and Ibn 'Abbas's view that it means a command is similar. According to al-Farra', ṭā'if is specifically a matter that comes by night. Ibn Jurayj said that this was a fiery flame (ʿunuqan min nār) that came out of the valley of their garden. It was also said that the ṭā'if was Jibril (ʿalayhi al-salām), who uprooted the garden, circled it around the town, and then set it down near Makkah, where the city of al-Ta'if is today, and that is why it was named after al-Ta'if. There is no other town in the land of the Hijaz that has water, trees and grapes besides it. In my view this does not hold, just as the claim that the city of al-Ta'if was originally in al-Sham and God moved it to the Hijaz through the prayer of Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salām) does not hold, and likewise the claim that it circled over the water during the Flood. If it were said that all of that is on its apparent meaning, it is a tale of fable, it would not be counted a fable. Al-Nakha'i read ﴿طَيْفٌ﴾ (ṭayf, "a phantom"). ﴿مِن رَبِّكَ﴾ means coming from His side, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿وهم نائِمُونَ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is that it came to them at night, as narrated from Qatadah. It was also said that the meaning is that they were in complete heedlessness of what the decrees had brought about. The first view is more apparent in terms of the preceding and following context.

﴿So it became like the sarim﴾: like a garden whose fruit has been cut off, so that nothing remains in it. Here *fa'il* is used in the sense of *maf'ul* (the Arabic *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, i.e. "cut" rather than "one who cuts"). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Like black ashes." This meaning is the dialect of Khuzayma (a tribe whose speech is cited as a linguistic authority). Also from him: the *sarim* is a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing.

Mu'arraj said: "Like a sand-dune that has been cut off from the main body of sand, and it produces nothing of benefit." Mundhir, al-Farra' and a group said: the *sarim* is the night, and the meaning is that it became burnt, resembling the night in its blackness. al-Thawri said: "Like the morning, from the point of view that it became white, like cut (harvested) crops." Some said: each of the night and the day is called *sarim*, because each is cut off from the other and separated from it.

﴿Then they called out to one another﴾ — each one calling to the others — ﴿early in the morning﴾, in accordance with their previous oath, ﴿Go out early to your tilth﴾, i.e., go out to your orchard, ﴿if you are going to harvest it﴾, i.e., intending to cut the fruit and gather it. Here ﴿أنِ﴾ (an, "that") is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and ﴿اغْدُوا﴾ (ighdu, "go out early") means "go out" (ukhruju). Alternatively, the meaning is "go out early" with ﴿أنِ﴾ being a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, and a governing preposition is understood before both of them; according to the more correct view, it may be connected to the imperative. ﴿عَلى حَرْثِكُمْ﴾ — ﴿حَرْثِكُمْ﴾ (harthikum, "your tilth") — is understood as your garden. ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صارِمِينَ﴾ — ﴿صارِمِينَ﴾ (sarimin, "those intending to harvest") — means those who intend to cut and harvest the fruit, so go out early. It has been said that it may mean "if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion," from their saying "a sharp sword" (sayfun sarimun), but this is not the case.

The apparent meaning of the words of Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) is that ghada (to go out early) means bakara (to set out in the morning), which takes ila (to), but here it is construed with ʿala (on) because ghada is implicitly given the sense of iqbal (turning toward), as in their saying: "he is fed upon (yughaddā ʿalayhi) with the bowl and is taken to graze (yuraḥ)," i.e., "turn toward your tilth early in the morning." It is also possible that it derives from ghada ʿalayhi, meaning "to raid upon him" (ghara), in which case their early departure to cut the fruit is likened to an army's raid upon something, because the sense of dominance and seizing (al-istiʿlaʾ wa-l-istiʾlaʾ) is present in it, namely cutting and severing. There would then be an implicit metaphor (istiʿarah tabaʿiyyah), and he also allowed that the metaphor be considered a representational metaphor (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah).

Abu Hayyan said: "What I have in memory is that ghada takes ʿala, as in his saying:

"And we have indeed gone out upon a band of noble men, drunk, having whatever we wish."

Likewise bakr, its synonym, takes it, as in his saying:

"I set out toward him at morning, and I saw him sitting before him, with his blamers at al-Sarim."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 68, verses 23–24:

﴿So they set off, whispering to one another.﴾ That is, they consult among themselves in a manner of *mukhafata* (hushed, secret speech). *Khafā* with a fatha on the *fā'* (*khafā*), *khafat*, and *khafad*, all three, carry the meaning of concealing. From this root comes *al-khafdūd* for the bat (*al-khuffāsh*), and *al-khafūd* for the she-camel that casts her offspring before its form has become clear.

﴿That no needy person shall enter it today against you.﴾ *Anna* (that) is either an explanatory particle (*mufassira*), because the whispering contains the sense of saying, or a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*), and the implied phrase is "that." The first view is supported by the *qirāʾa* (recitation variant) of ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn Abī ʿAbla, which omit it. On that basis it is said that it is with the implied verb "say." It is also said that the governing word is *yatakhāfatūn* (they whisper), since it includes the sense of saying; this is the Kufan position on it and on similar constructions. Whichever it is, the purpose of prohibiting the needy person from entering is to stress the prohibition against enabling him to enter, like the saying "I shall not see you here."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 25:

﴿And they set off early in the morning with determination (ḥard)﴾. That is, with prevention (man'), as Abu 'Ubayd and others said, from the expression of the Arabs: ḥāradat al-ibil (the camels' milk decreased) when their milk became scant, and ḥāradat al-sanah (the year became scant) when its rain and goodness diminished. The prepositional phrase ʿalā ḥardin is connected to the words of the Exalted ﴿capable﴾ (qādirīna). It was placed first for restriction (ḥaṣr) and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawāṣil). The meaning is: "And they set off capable of prevention only." The sense is that they resolved to prevent the poor from benefiting and sought to deprive them and afflict them, while they were capable of benefiting them. So they set off in a state in which they were capable of nothing but prevention and deprivation. That is because they sought to deprive the poor, and so they hastened their own deprivation. Or, they set off upon the withering of their garden and the going of its goodness, instead of being capable of gaining its produce and benefits; that is, they set off having brought deprivation upon themselves in place of being capable of benefiting. The restriction on the first interpretation is real (ḥaqīqī), and on this one it is relative (idāfī) with respect to their benefiting from their garden, and the deprivation upon it is specific to them.

It is also permitted that ﴿ʿalā ḥardin﴾ be connected to ghadawā (they set off), and the intended meaning of ḥard is the ḥard of the garden. It was brought in as a counterpart (mushākala) to ḥarth (tilling), as if, when they said ﴿Set off early to your tilling﴾ while their intention was corrupt, God the Exalted punished them by making their garden wither and depriving them of its goodness. So they did not set off to tilling, but set off to ḥard. And ﴿qādirīna﴾ is, by inversion of speech, for sarcasm (tahakkum): that is, capable of what they had resolved upon of harvesting and depriving the poor.

It has been said that ḥard is with a fatha on the rāʾ, and it has been read that way. It means anger and rage, as Abu Naṣr Aḥmad ibn Ḥātim, companion of al-Aṣmaʿī, said, and he recited:

When the swift horses came running, filled with rage and ḥard.

That is, they were capable only of provoking one another to anger, as in the words of the Exalted ﴿Then some of them turned to others, blaming one another﴾ [al-Qalam: 30]. This was narrated from Sufyan and al-Suddi. The restriction is real but figurative (ḥaqīqī iddiʿāʾī) or relative (idāfī). It has also been said that it means intent and haste, and he recited:

A flood came from the command of God ∗∗∗ hastening with the haste of a garden that yields little.

That is, they set off intending their garden swiftly, capable in their own estimation of harvesting it. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. So ﴿ʿalā ḥardin﴾ is a stationary adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr), a circumstantial (ḥāl) of the pronoun in (ghadawā), and (qādirīna) is also a circumstantial, except that it is a prospective circumstantial (ḥāl muqaddara), according to what has been said. It has been said that it is a real circumstantial, based on the restriction with ʿinda anfusihim (in their own estimation). It was restricted by this because the fruits of their garden were destroyed, so they had no capability to harvest them, and they had perished.

Al-Azhari said: ḥardin is the name of their village. In a report from al-Suddi, it is the name of their garden. I do not think that is intended. It has also been said that ḥard means isolation (infirād). One says: "He withdrew (ḥarada) from his people" when he moved away from them and settled alone. And a star that is ḥarūd is one that stands apart from the stars. The meaning is: they set off to their garden in isolation from the poor, none of them being with them, capable of harvesting it; and this is of the category of sarcasm. It has also been said that qādirīna, on this view, is from qadar in the sense of constriction (taḍyīq), that is, constricting the poor, since they deprived them of what their father used to grant them from it. And this is a prospective circumstantial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verses 26–27:

﴿When they saw it﴾, at the very first moment their gaze fell upon it, ﴿they said: "Indeed we have gone astray"﴾, (having lost) the way to our garden, and it was not it. This is what Qatadah said. It was also said that ﴿"we have gone astray"﴾ means they strayed from what is right in our going out with the intention of withholding (the due) from the poor, but this is not the correct view.

﴿"Nay, we are deprived"﴾. They said this after they reflected, and came to know the reality of the matter, turning away from their first statement; that is, "We are not astray; rather, ﴿we are deprived﴾, we have been deprived of its good because of our own transgression against ourselves."

﴿Said the most moderate of them﴾, meaning the best and most judicious of them in intellect and opinion, or the middle one in age. ﴿Did I not tell you: why do you not glorify [God]?﴾, meaning: why do you not remember God Most High and repent to Him for the corruption of your intention? He had told them, when they resolved upon that, "Remember God Most High and repent to Him from this wicked intention immediately, and hasten to cut off its evil before the punishment descends." But they disobeyed him, so he reproached them. What points to this meaning is the saying of God Most High: ﴿They said: Glory be to our Lord! Indeed we were wrongdoers﴾, because glorifying (tasbih) is the remembrance of God Most High, and "indeed we were..." etc. is regret and acknowledgment of sin, and so it is repentance. The apparent meaning is that they spoke with what would have prompted them to speak upon committing the sin, but only after the destruction of the garden (al-Basrah, i.e., the orchard). It has also been said that what is meant by glorifying is the exception (istithna', the saying "if God wills"), since both share the sense of exalting God, Mighty and Majestic, because making an exception is entrusting the matter to Him, Glorified is He, and glorifying is declaring Him far above imperfection, and each of entrusting and declaring Him free of imperfection is an exaltation. So it is as if it were said: "Did I not tell you: why do you not make the exception," i.e., why do you not say, "if God Most High wills."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Juraij, and it is related in al-Bahr from Mujahid and Abu Salih that both of them said: Their exception at that time was the glorifying, just as we say today "if God Most High wills." Some of the Hanafi scholars (the Hanafiyyah, the Hanafi school of law) made it the exception of the present day, so that according to him, if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced, Glory be to God," she is not divorced. He attributed this to the Imam Ibn al-Humam and claimed that he stated it in his fatwas. It has been justified by saying that what is meant by "Glory be to God" in what was mentioned is "I declare God, Mighty and Majestic, free from creating what is hateful to Him," and that is divorce, for it has been reported that the most hateful of lawful things to God Most High is divorce. But some later scholars denied the attribution of this to that earlier Imam, and denied that he had any fatwas.

The aforementioned justification has been objected to in the same way it was objected to, and by my life, it is too weak to deserve objection. As for me, I say that more fitting than it is the statement of al-Nahhas in justifying the placing of glorifying in the position of the exception: that the meaning is declaring God Most High free from anything coming to be except by His will. It may be said: perhaps whoever said that built the matter upon the soundness of what has been transmitted, and that the law of those before us is law for us when God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) relate it to us without disapproval. This, with its flaws, is better than what has been said in justifying it, as is not hidden. It has also been said: the meaning is "why do you not seek forgiveness," and the manner of the figurative usage is known from what has preceded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verses 30–31:

﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ They blamed one another, for among them was one who had advised that course, and among them were those who approved of it, among them those who remained silent, content with it, and among them those who disapproved of it. The attribution of the actions in what preceded to all of them does not preclude this, as is known in more than one place. ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were transgressors.﴾ Exceeding the limits of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 32:

﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it﴾, that is, He will grant us in its place, through the blessing of repentance and acknowledging the sin, ﴿something better than it﴾, that is, than that garden. ﴿Indeed, to our Lord﴾ alone, not to other than Him, glorified is He, ﴿we are turning eagerly﴾, hoping for pardon and seeking good. ("Ila" [to]) is used to denote the endpoint of the desire, or because it includes the meaning of returning. It is narrated from Mujahid that they repented and were given in exchange something better than it. It is also narrated that they made a pact among themselves and said: "If Allah, exalted is He, gives us something better than it, we will surely act as our father acted." So they called upon Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and humbled themselves before Him, glorified is He, and Allah, exalted is He, gave them, that very night, something better than it. Ibn Mas'ud said: "It has reached me that the people called upon Allah, exalted is He, and were sincere, and Allah, exalted is He, knew their truthfulness, so He gave them in its place a garden called al-Hayawan (the Living), in which there are grapes, one cluster of which is carried on a mule." Abu Khalid al-Yamani said: "I saw that garden, and every cluster in it was like a standing black man." Abu Hayyan preferred the view that they were believers who committed a sin and repented. It is related from some that they were from the People of the Book. And it is related from al-Tastuari that most of them say they repented and were sincere. Al-Hasan hesitated concerning their faith, and said: "I do not know whether their saying ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are turning eagerly﴾ was faith, or was in the manner of what the polytheists say when hardship befalls them."

Qatada was asked about them: were they among the People of the Garden or among the People of the Fire? He said to the questioner: "You have burdened me with a hard question out of obstinacy." Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read «yubaddilana» with doubled letter (shaddah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 33:

﴿Such is the punishment﴾. It is a clause consisting of a subject and a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), used to convey restriction (qasr), and the alif-lam (al) in al-'adhab is for prior reference (al-'ahd). That is: the like of that punishment with which We tested the people of Makkah through severe drought, and the companions of the garden, is the punishment of this world, as has been narrated. It has been said that the statement comes as a warning to them, as if, when the Exalted forbade him from obeying the disbelievers, especially their leaders, He mentioned that their rebellion was due to the wealth and children they had been given. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, followed this by saying that if these two do not give thanks to the Benefactor, the state of their possessor will end up in the state of the companions of the garden. Implicit in this is that corrupt intention and withholding from the poor, when they lead to what was mentioned, then opposing the Truth, the Exalted, by opposing one who is over His creation and the most noble of the existents, and severing one's kinship ties, is more likely to bring the people of Makkah to ruin.

And the statement of the Exalted: ﴿But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾, that is, greater and more severe, a warning against opposition in a more eloquent manner. And the statement of the Glorified: ﴿If only they knew﴾ reproaches them for heedlessness, that is: if they were among the people of knowledge, they would know that it is greater, and they would take caution from it.

Surely for those who are mindful (of disbelief, as in al-Bahr, or of it and of sins, as in al-Irshad) ﴿with their Lord﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, for it is specific to Him, mighty and majestic, since none other disposes of it, or in a nearness He has sanctified, ﴿are Gardens of Bliss﴾: gardens in which there is nothing but pure bliss, free from any admixture of what would spoil it, such as turbidities and the fear of its ending. The restriction (qasr) is drawn from the annexation to ﴿bliss﴾, because it conveys distinction from the gardens of this world, and an implicit contrast that the gardens of this world are predominantly marked by disturbance:

"You were formed upon turbidity, yet you seek it pure, free from filths and troubles."

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 68, verses 35–36:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it regarding the triumph of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), and a refutation of what the disbelievers say when they hear the discourse about the Hereafter and what God Exalted has promised, if it is true that we will be resurrected, as Muhammad (ﷺ) and those with him claim. Our condition and theirs is nothing but like their condition in this world; they have not surpassed us, nor have they been given preference over us, and at most their situation is that they are equal to us. The hamza is for denial (al-inkar), and the fa' is for conjunction (al-'atf), and the conjunction is upon an implied element that the speech requires, that is: so the ruler deviates in judgment, and thus makes the Muslims like the disbelievers. Then, by way of iltifat (shift of address), it was said to them, for the emphasis and intensification of the refutation, ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ as an expression of wonder at their judgment and a declaration of its improbability, and an announcement that it cannot proceed from a rational person, since the meaning of "ma lakum" is: what has come upon you of defect of thought and corruption of opinion?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verses 37–38:

﴿Or do you have a Book﴾ sent down from the heaven, ﴿in which﴾ (fīhi), i.e., in the Book, the prepositional phrase being connected to His statement, exalted is He, ﴿you study﴾, i.e., you read in it; and the clause is a qualifier of "a Book." It is also permissible that "fīhi" be connected to the complement of the predicate, or that it be the qualifier, with the pronoun referring to the ruling or the command. ﴿And you study﴾ is either a resumptive clause or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of address. And His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, for you therein is what you choose﴾, i.e., for what you choose and desire. It is said: "takhayyara al-shay'" and "ikhtāra-hu," meaning he took its best part (khayyir-hu), and it has become common in taking whatever one wants, unrestrictedly. The object of ﴿you study﴾ is the studied matter, since it is the thing studied, so it occupies the position of a singular noun. Its original form was: "anna lakum fīhi mā takhayyarūn," with the hamza of "anna" vowelled with a fatḥa and the lām omitted from its predicate. When the lām was introduced, the hamza was given a kasra and the verb was suspended from acting. For this reason it has been said that it is necessary to include in "tadrusūn" the meaning of knowledge (al-'ilm), so that governance (al-'amal) operates in it in the sentences and the suspension (al-ta'līq).

It is also permissible that this be a quotation of what is studied, as it stands, so that it is precisely the word "Book" without conversion from fatḥa to kasra. The pronoun of "fīhi," according to the first view, refers to the Book, and it is repeated for emphasis. According to this, it refers to their affair or to the ruling, so that the meaning is: what is written in the Book, or the ruling, or the command, is entrusted to them. Thus the statement of the author of al-Taqrib is refuted, that the word "fīhi" does not support this, since "fīhi" has already been sufficient at first without any need to make the pronoun of "fīhi" refer to the Day of Resurrection by the context, or to the place indicated by His statement, ﴿with their Lord﴾. On the resumptive reading, it also refers to the ruling. It is also permissible to stop at "tadrusūn," with the statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, for you﴾ etc. being a resumptive clause in the sense: if you have a Book, then for you therein is what you choose. And this, as you see, is weak.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿Or do you have﴾ etc. is a counterpart to what precedes it, in view of the resultant meaning, since its import is: has your intellect been so corrupted that I have judged you by this, or has a Book come to you
صفحة 34
in which your choice and the delegation of the affair to you are present? Ṭalḥa and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "an lakum" with a fatḥa on the hamza, and the lām in "lamā" is extra, like the reading of one who read "alā innahum la-ya'kulūn al-ṭa'ām" with a fatḥa on the hamza of "annahum." Al-A'raj read "an lakum" with an interrogative, on the resumptive basis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 39:

﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us﴾ — i.e., oaths of swearing. It has also been explained as covenants, and the application of the term "oaths" (iyman) to them is either by applying the part to the whole (al-juz' 'ala al-kull) or the necessary to that which it necessitates (al-lazim 'ala al-malzum). ﴿Binding﴾ — i.e., the utmost possible; the meaning is "reaching their completion in emphasis." Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "bali‘ah" (بالِغَةً) in the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun concealed in ("upon Us") or ("for you"). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "it is from the oath-words, since it is specified by the description," but this is remote. ﴿Until the Day of Resurrection﴾ — this is connected to the implied element in ("for you"), meaning: they remain valid for you until the Day of Resurrection, and you will not be released from their obligation except on that day, when We judge you and give you what you judge. Or it is connected to "binding," meaning: oaths that reach that day and end at it, complete, none of which has been voided. Thus "until" (ila), on the first view, indicates the endpoint of the established state implied in the adverbial phrase, so it is like the term of a debt; and on the second view it indicates the endpoint of reaching, so it is a restriction on the oath, meaning an emphatic oath that does not dissolve until that day. It is not about postponing the thing sworn to in any way, since "binding" has no bearing on the thing sworn to, so reflect on this.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, for you is what you judge﴾ is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of "Or do you have oaths upon Us" is "Or have We sworn to you." This runs according to the interpretation of oaths as covenants, since a covenant is like an oath with no difference, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. Al-A'raj read "aana lakum" (آنَ لَكُمْ) also as an interrogative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verses 40–41:

"Ask them" (﴿سَلْهُمْ﴾) is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab) and a directing of the speech to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by removing them from the rank of being addressed. That is, "Ask them, rebuking them," ﴿which of them will stand surety for that﴾ external judgment that lies outside the circle of reason, ﴿a guarantor﴾, one who stands up to vouch for its correctness. The interrogative clause is in the position of the second object (al-ma'mul al-thani) of sal, and according to Abu Hayyan and a group of scholars the verb is suspended (mu'allaq) from it because of the interrogative (al-istifham) that follows. The question being treated as occupying the place of knowledge, since it is a cause of obtaining it, is also possible.

﴿Or do they have partners﴾ who share in this claim and follow their path? ﴿Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful﴾ in their claim, since there is at least the minimum of imitation (taqlid). Exalted and glorified is He, in these verses, has drawn attention to negating everything by which they could attach themselves to establish their claim. He, exalted is His majesty, drew attention to negating rational proof (al-dalil al-'aqli) by His saying, ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾; and to negating transmitted proof (al-dalil al-naqli) by His saying, ﴿Or do you have a Book﴾, and so on; and to negating that God had promised them this, and the promise of the Generous is a debt, by His saying, ﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us﴾, and so on; and to negating imitation, which is weaker than the threads of a spider's web, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Or do they have partners﴾.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "Or do they have gods whom they count as partners in divinity, which would make them like the Muslims in the Hereafter?"

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Ablah read "fa-l-ya'tu bi-shirkihim" (then let them bring their partnership), and what is meant by it is the same as what is meant by "shuraka'ihim" (their partners).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 42:**

﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered﴾ is connected to His saying, ﴿then let them come﴾, according to both views. It may also be connected to an implied verb such as "remember," or to "such and such," or to "khashi'a" (humbled), or to "tarhaquhum" (will overcome them). Whichever is the case, the "day" here is, according to the majority of scholars, the Day of Resurrection. The *saq* (shin, or lower leg) is the part above the foot. Uncovering it and rolling up the garment from it is a figure of speech (*mathal*) for the severity of a matter and the difficulty of a calamity, to the point that it is used in contexts where no "shin" can be imagined at all, as in the words of Hatim:

*He is a brother of war: if war bites him, he bites back; and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up.*

And the words of the rajaz poet:

*I marvel at myself and at my fear of it, and at the horses' holding back from their provisions,*

*in a year that uncovered its shin, red, stripping the flesh from its bones.*

Its origin is the rolling up of the shins by veiled women when fleeing, for they do not do so except when the calamity is great and the matter is severe, so that they forget to cover themselves with the hem of modesty. This is also the view of Mujahid, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ikrimah, and a group of others. It has also been narrated from Ibn Abbas that Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related through Ikrimah that he was asked about this, and he said: "If something of the Qur'an is obscure to you, seek it in poetry, for it is the register (*diwan*) of the Arabs. Have you not heard the words of the poet:

*Patience, Anaq! Indeed it is an evil that remains. Your people have already established for me the striking of necks.*

*And war has stood up with us on its shin."*

The reports from him, may Allah be pleased with him, to this effect are numerous. It has also been said that the *saq* of a thing is its root upon which its stability depends, like the trunk of a tree or the shin of a person. The meaning is: the Day when the root of the matter is uncovered, so that the realities and origins of affairs become manifest and are seen with the eye. The words of al-Rabi' ibn Anas point to this, for Abd ibn Humayd related from him that he said regarding this: "The Day when the veil is removed." Similarly, al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas, also, that he said: "When the matter is uncovered and the deeds become visible." On this meaning, there is an explicit metaphor (*isti'ara tasrihiyya*) in "shin," and there is another figurative usage in "uncovering," or it is a *tarshih* (a supporting element that completes a metaphor) for the metaphor, while "shin" remains on its literal meaning. The indefinite form of *saq* (*sa-qin*) is said to be for magnification (*tahwil*) according to the first view, and for exaltation (*ta'zim*) according to the second.

It has been said that neither of these two aspects is to be considered on the first view, because the discourse in it is an analogy (*tamthil*), and in an analogy the individual words are not examined at all. Some scholars held that the intended "shin" is the shin of Allah, glory be to Him, and that the verse is among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses). They cited in support of this what was related by al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Sa'id, who said: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: 'Our Lord will uncover His shin, and every believing man and woman will prostrate to Him. Those who used to prostrate in the world for show and reputation will remain; they will go to prostrate, but their backs will become one solid plate.'"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr denied this. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he was asked about the verse, and he became extremely angry and said: "Indeed, some people claim that Allah, glory be to Him, uncovers His shin, whereas He only uncovers a severe matter." On this, the hadith is also interpreted as referring to a severe matter, and its attribution to Him, mighty and majestic, is for the magnification of its affair, and that it is a matter that no one other than Him, mighty and majestic, is capable of. The adepts of the inner dimension among the Sufis say that it is to be taken in its apparent sense, and they claim that this happens at the time of the "manifestation of form" (*tajalli suwari*).

On this interpretation they also relied on what Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in *al-Ru'ya*, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and others, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allah will gather the people on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will descend in shadows of clouds, and a caller will call out: 'O people! Are you not content with your Lord, who created you, formed you, and provided for you, that He should turn each person toward what he used to worship in the world, and that he should follow it? Is that not justice from your Lord?' They will say: 'Yes.' He will say: 'Let each one of you go to what he used to follow in the world.' And there will be presented to them what they used to worship in the world, and there will be presented to those who used to worship Jesus, peace be upon him, the devil of Jesus; likewise, there will be presented to those who used to worship Uzayr, until the tree, the twig, and the stone are presented to them. The people of Islam will remain kneeling, and the Lord, mighty and majestic, will manifest Himself to them, and it will be said to them: 'What is the matter with you? You have not gone as the people have gone.' They will say: 'Indeed, we have a Lord whom we have not seen yet.' He will say: 'By what will you recognize your Lord if you see Him?' They will say: 'Between us and Him is a sign: if we see Him, we will know Him.' He will say: 'And what is it?' They will say: 'He will uncover His shin.' Then He will uncover it at that moment..." — the hadith.

This hadith and its like are, according to the early generation (*salaf*), among the *mutashabih*. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Ablah read *yukshafu* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, in the active voice (*mabniyyan lil-fa'il*), and this is also a transmission from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Hurmuz read *nakshifu* with a *nun*. It was also read as *yukshifu* with a *ya'* (below) and *damma* on it, with a *kasra* on the *shin*, from *aksha'a*, meaning "he entered into uncovering," and from it comes *iksh'if al-rijl* ("uncover the leg"), so that he becomes *mukashshaf*, meaning his upper lip has been turned back.

It was also read as *takshifu* with a *ta'* (above) and in the active voice, where the pronoun refers to the Hour known from the mention of the Day of Resurrection, or to the state known from the context (*dalalat al-hal*). It was also read in the passive voice, with the pronoun referring to the Hour or to the state. It was objected to this reading that the original would then be: "Allah uncovers the Hour from its shin," for example. If this were said, it would not be correct, because it requires the presentation of a shin and the removal of the Hour, as one says: "She uncovered the veil from her face," whereas the Hour is not a covering over the shin so that it could be uncovered. It was answered that it was made a covering as an exaggeration, because the veiled woman exerts herself to the utmost in concealment, so that she is as though she were the covering itself, and so it is said, "The Hour uncovers." This is like your saying, "I uncovered Zayd from his ignorance," when you exaggerate in displaying his ignorance, because it was a covering over his ignorance, concealing his faults; then you revealed it and made it manifest, so that it was not hidden from anyone. It was said in response to this that the removal in that case is figurative (*id'a'i*), and the artificiality of this is not hidden. Nor is any weight to be given to the invented example that was mentioned. Less artificial than it is the view of making ﴿from a shin﴾ a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for the concealed pronoun in the verb, after the omission of the preposition from it.

The original would be "he uncovers from it," that is, from the Hour or the state. The preposition was dropped and the pronoun became concealed. It was objected to this that substituting a prepositional phrase for a nominative pronoun is not valid according to the rules of Arabic grammar, so it is "a bundle of herbs on top of a bundle" (*digh' 'ala ibala*), an artificiality upon an artificiality. It was also said that ﴿from a shin﴾ is the deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*). It was objected that the verb ought to be masculine, as in *sarafa 'an Hind* ("he turned away from Hind") and *murra bi Da'd* ("he passed by Da'd").

﴿And they will be called to prostrate﴾, as a rebuke and reproach for their neglect of it in the world, and as a grief-causing reproof for their negligence in this. ﴿But they will not be able﴾, because the ability to do so has gone. This implies that they intend it, but it does not come about for them. On the authority of Ibn Mas'ud: "Their backs will be made rigid," that is, they will be turned into bones without joints that do not bend when raised or lowered. This was mentioned in the hadith of al-Bukhari and those with him, "what they heard." And in another hadith: "The backs of the hypocrites and the disbelievers will become like the horns of cows, one solid bone."

The apparent view is that the one who calls is Allah, exalted, or the angel. It has been said that it is what they see of the prostration of the believers. Abu Muslim cited this verse as evidence that the Day of uncovering is in this world, saying: "Because He, exalted, said, 'and they will be called to prostrate,' whereas on the Day of Resurrection there is no worship and no obligation." Therefore it is meant either as the last days of a person's life in this world, when he sees the angels, or as the time of illness, old age, and the miracle. This is refuted by what we have indicated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 43:

﴿Their eyes downcast﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of ﴿they are called﴾, on the basis that ﴿their eyes﴾ is raised by it as the agent (fa'iliyya). Ascribing humility (khushu') to the eyes is because its effect is manifest in them. (Tarhaquhum) means (talhaquhum) overtakes them and covers them. (Dhilla) means severe ﴿humiliation﴾. ﴿And they used to be called to prostration﴾ in the world; the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun for added emphasis (taqrir). Or, because what is meant by it is the obligatory prayers, as al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi said; or all acts of obedience, as has been said. The call (da'wa) is the call of obligation (taklif). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: they used to hear the adhan and the call to prayer and would not respond. ﴿And they were sound﴾ (salimun), able to do it in the strongest way; that is, they would not respond to it and would refuse it. The mention of this was omitted, relying on its being evident.

﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾. That is, since their state is as you have heard, leave to Me everyone who denies the Qur'an, and ask Me to suffice you, for in Me is what will relieve your mind and free your heart from concern. This is from eloquent speech, indicating that the speaker is confident of being able to fulfil, to the utmost, what the addressee desires and even more than that. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) verified this with the following substance: whoever asks someone to suffice him leaves the matter to that person, otherwise it would be seeking help (isti'anah) and not seeking sufficiency (istikfa', asking to be sufficed). So the consequent (al-radif), namely the leaving-alone (al-takhliyah), was placed in the position of seeking sufficiency, as in the phrase "leave him and Himself" (wa-in yadhuruhu wa-iyyahu), for emphasis (mubalaghah) and to indicate complete sufficiency. How could it be otherwise, when this One who suffices is the one asked to suffice?

It has been said: the saying "dharni" (leave Me) and the expression of leaving off seeking sufficiency in the form of prohibition are an emphasis upon emphasis. Had He not been highly confident of His ability to fulfil the matter to the fullest extent, and beyond what revolves in the mind of the one seeking sufficiency, there would be no way for the request to be made in this most eloquent manner.

"Man" (ومن) is in the accusative position, either as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the object in "dharni," or as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ah). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We shall draw them on step by step﴾ (sa-nastadrijuhum), is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) given to explain in detail the manner of the punishment, which is implied in general terms by the preceding statement. The pronoun refers to "man," and the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular in "yukadhdhibu" (denies) is used in view of its wording. That is, We shall bring them down to punishment degree by degree, through respite, continued health and increase of blessing, ﴿from where they do not know﴾ that this is a gradual drawing (istidraj). Rather, they assume that this is a privilege granted to them and a favour over the believers, while in fact it is the cause of their destruction.

And I give them respite. Indeed, My plan is firm.

I give them respite (wa-umli lahum): I grant them time, so that they increase in sin, while they suppose that this is because God wishes good for them. "Indeed, My plan is firm" (inna kaydi matin): it cannot be repelled by anything. Calling this a "plan" (kayd) is a kind of stratagem (ihtiyal) because it is in its outward form: God, glory be to Him, does with them what appears to be benefit for them, while His real intention by it is harm, since He knows the corruption of their nature and their persistence in disbelief and ingratitude.

﴿Or do you ask them﴾ for reward for conveying and guiding, ﴿a wage﴾ in worldly terms, ﴿so that they are﴾ for that reason ﴿burdened with debt﴾, i.e., a financial penalty, ﴿heavily laden﴾, i.e., charged with a heavy burden, ﴿so they turn away from you.﴾ This sentence, according to what Ibn al-Shaykh said, is conjoined to His, exalted is He, saying ﴿Or do they have partners?﴾
