Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 47:

﴿Or do they have the unseen (al-ghayb), so that they write (it down)?﴾ That is, the things that are unseen (al-mughayyabat), or (it refers to) the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). The term "the unseen" (al-ghayb) is applied to it metaphorically, because it is the place where the unseen things are written, or because their forms appear in it, based on the well-known disagreement concerning this matter. The indicator (al-qarinah) is the words ﴿so they write﴾, meaning what they judge by, and by that they dispense with your knowledge.

﴿So be patient with the decree of your Lord﴾, that is, with His delaying them and postponing your victory over them. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to invoke curses against Thaqif when they harmed him, at the time when he (ﷺ) presented himself to the tribes in Makkah. Then this was revealed. It has also been said that he (ﷺ) wished to invoke curses against those who fled at Uhud, when the situation became severe for the Muslims, and then this was revealed. According to this view, the verse is Madani (revealed in Madinah). ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾: he is Yunus (peace be upon him), just as the one meant by "Dhu al-Nun" (the man of the fish). However, he distinguished between dhi (ذِي) and sahib (صاحِب), on the basis that dhi is more emphatic than sahib. Ibn Hajar said: this is because dhi requires the magnification of what it is annexed to and of what it describes, unlike sahib. For this reason, in the context of praising Yunus (peace be upon him), He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And Dha al-Nun﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87], while the prohibition against following him says: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾, since al-Nun, because it was made the opening of a surah, is more majestic and more noble than the word al-hut (the fish). Al-Sarminiyy transmitted something similar from the scholar al-Suhayli. Others distinguished in ways other than this, which are mentioned in our marginal notes on Ibn Isam's treatise on the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan, the science of rhetorical expression).

(إذْ) [when]: he called out in the belly of the fish, ﴿while he was distressed﴾, that is, filled with rage against his people because they did not believe when he called them to faith. It derives from kazm al-siqa', meaning filling the water-skin when it is full, and it is used in this sense in the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"You, because of your love for Mayy, are concealing a sorrow, an anguish of the heart, a wounded heart, filled with grief."

The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in nada (called out), and the prohibition is directed at this clause, not at the calling out itself, for the calling out is a commendable act of supplication. For this reason the one called out to is not mentioned. The word (إذْ) is in the accusative, governed by an omitted annexed noun (mudaf mahdhuf), meaning: "Let your state not be like his state at the time of his calling out," that is, let there not be found in you what was found in him of impatience and displeasure, lest you be afflicted with something like his affliction (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 49:

﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him﴾, which is His granting him success in repentance and its acceptance from him. It is also read as "raḥmah" (mercy). The verb is masculine in both readings because the subject is feminine only metaphorically, and there is a separating pronoun. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ibn ʿAbbas read "tadārakat-hu" with the feminine ta' (tāʾ al-taʾnīth). Ibn Hurmuz, al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "﴿tadārakahu﴾" with a shaddah on the dal (dāl). Its original form is "tatadārakahu," so the ta' was changed to dal and the first dal was assimilated into the second dal (idghām). The intended meaning is the narration of a past state, as if to say: had it not been that it was being said of him "tatadārakuhu." ﴿He would have been cast out onto the bare land﴾, that is, onto land empty of trees, in this world. It was also said: onto the bare plain of the Resurrection, based on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And had he not been of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143, 144]. Its remoteness is not hidden. ﴿While he was blameworthy﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the nominative subject of "nubidha" (was cast out), and on it depends the answer of "lawla" (had not), because the intended meaning is the prevention of his being cast out in a blameworthy state; otherwise the casting out had already occurred. This indicates that his state was contrary to blame. The purpose is that the state of being cast out and abandoned was different from the state of being sick and at the beginning, based on His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142]. In al-Irshad it is stated that the conditional sentence is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) that comes to explain that what is prohibited is a dreaded matter which entails a harmful consequence (ghā'ilah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 50:

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon something implied, meaning: a favour from his Lord overtook him. (﴿Fa-ijtabahu﴾) means: He chose him (iṣṭafāhu), by Him, the Mighty and Majestic, returning revelation (al-waḥy) to him and sending him to a hundred thousand or more. It is also said: He made him a prophet (istanbaʾahu), if it is sound that he had not been a prophet before this event, and that he was only a messenger (rasūl) to some of the messengers in the land of Syria. ﴿So He made him among the righteous﴾ means among the perfect in righteousness (al-kāmilīn fi al-ṣalāḥ), by His, the Glorified's, protecting him from doing an act whose abandonment would be better. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that the making him among the righteous is an explanation of the choosing (al-ijtibāʾ). It is said that "the righteous" (al-ṣāliḥīn) has been interpreted as the prophets, and this is based on the view that he had not been a prophet before the event. The verse has been cited as evidence for the creation of acts (khalq al-afʿāl), because His making him righteous is by making his righteousness and creating it in him, and this is among the acts, and there is no one who makes a distinction. The Muʿtazila interpret that in one place as an informing of his righteousness, and in another as the kindness (luṭf) shown to him until he became righteous. Since it is possible that what is meant by "the righteous" is the prophets, as has been said, the verse does not indicate more than that prophethood is something made (majʿūlah), and this is among what both groups agree upon, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 51:

﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes﴾. "In" (إنْ) here is the light (mukhaffafah, lightened) form, and the lam is its indicator, since it does not enter after a negating particle; for this reason it is called al-fariqah (the distinguishing particle) by convention among the grammarians. The meaning is that, because of the intensity of their enmity, they look at you sidelong, such that they almost make your foot slip, so that they strike you down. This is from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocks me down, or almost eats me," meaning: if his look were able to knock me down or to devour me, he would do it. It is made an exaggeration of their enmity, to the point that it seems to have spread from the heart and the limbs into the glance, so that the glance itself came to act as a limb. They recited the words of the poet:

They exchange, when they meet in a place, a look that makes the feet of the steps slip.

Or it means that they almost strike you with the evil eye, for it is narrated that among Banu Asad there were men with the evil eye, and some of them wished to afflict the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so this was revealed.

Al-Kalbi said: A man among the Arabs would stay two or three days without eating, then he would lift the side of his tent and say: "I have never seen, today, camels or sheep better than these," and some of them would fall and perish. So the disbelievers proposed that he should afflict the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He answered them and recited:

Your people used to reckon you a lord, and I suppose that you are a lord who is struck by the evil eye.

So Allah the Exalted protected His Prophet (ﷺ) and revealed this verse. It has been said that reciting it averts the harm of the evil eye, and this is narrated from al-Hasan. In the Book of Rulings it is said that it is the basis for holding that the evil eye is real. The better course is to argue for this from what has been reported and authenticated through several chains: that the evil eye brings a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot; and from what Ahmad recorded with a chain whose narrators, as al-Haythami said, are trustworthy, from Abu Dharr, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed the evil eye causes a man to fall, by the permission of Allah the Exalted, until he climbs high and then throws himself down from it."

And besides that, there are many other hadiths. This belongs to the special properties of some souls, and it is for Allah the Exalted to single out whom He wills among them with what He wills. Its attribution to the eye is because the soul generally acts through it. The influence may also occur without it, by describing something to the one with the evil eye, so that his soul turns toward it and corrupts it. Whoever says that Allah the Exalted has established the custom of creating whatever He wills upon the encounter with the evil eye's gaze, with no influence at all, has closed to himself the door of causes, effects, means and results, and has opposed all the wise. Ibn al-Qayyim said this. Some of the proponents of natural philosophy said that a hidden (sumiyyah, poisonous) force proceeds from the eye and affects what it looks at, as explained in the commentary on Muslim. In my view, this does not hold regarding what one has not seen, nor regarding the kind of thing contained in the hadith of Abu Dharr mentioned just above, nor regarding a person striking his own eye, as al-Munawi related, for the viper is not killed by its own poison.

Among such reports is what al-Ghassani related: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik looked in a mirror, was pleased with himself, and said:

Muhammad (ﷺ) was a prophet, Abu Bakr was a truthful one, Umar was a discerner, Uthman was modest, Mu'awiyah was forbearing, Yazid was patient, Abd al-Malik was a administrator, al-Walid was a tyrant, and I am the young king, I am the young king. Before the month had passed over him, he died.

Similar to this is what has been said: that it belongs to the category of influence through the force known today as electrical force among modern mesmerists. It is established that some people repeatedly gaze at certain persons from their head down to their feet, and it knocks them down as if they had fainted; and perhaps one stands behind him, placing his fingers opposite the hollow of his head and directing his soul toward him, until his powers weaken and a sleep-like state overtakes him, and in that state he speaks things he would not speak at another time. I say no more than that it is among the effects of souls, and I do not specify how that is. The human soul is among the most wondrous of Allah's creations, the Mighty and Majestic, and many secrets and wonders are folded within it, at which minds are bewildered, and none denies them except a madman or an ignorant person. I cannot bring myself to deny the evil eye, given the abundance of hadiths concerning it and the observation of its effects across different ages, nor do I restrict it to evil souls, as has been said, for it may come from pure souls too.

It is well known that affliction does not occur together with disliking or hatred of the thing, but only together with admiring it. Al-Qushayri went to this view, and it seems he is pointing by this to a challenge to the soundness of the report here, because the disbelievers were hostile toward him (ﷺ), so affliction by the evil eye would not be possible for them. There is room for discussion in this.

The ruling on the one with the evil eye, according to al-Qadi Iyad, is that he should be avoided; and it is fitting for the imam to confine him and prevent him from mixing with people, to restrain his harm as far as possible, and to provide for him from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) at that time.

Furthermore, Nafi' recited "la-yuzliqunaka" with a fatha on the ya', from zalaqahu meaning azlaqahu (made him slip). Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, al-A'mash and Isa recited "la-yuzhiqunaka" with a ha' in place of the lam, meaning: "they would destroy you."

﴿When they hear the Reminder﴾: that is, at the time of their hearing the Qur'an, and this is because of the intensity of their hatred and envy when they hear it.

(Lamma), as we have indicated, is a temporal particle connected to "yuzliqunaka." Whoever said it is a particle of necessity for necessity holds that its response is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it: that is, "when they heard the Reminder, they almost made you slip." ﴿And they say﴾ out of the utmost of their bewilderment regarding his matter (ﷺ) and the extremity of their ignorance of the wonders of wise judgments and marvelous sciences contained within the Qur'an, and to repel people from him: ﴿Indeed, he is surely a madman﴾. And since the basis of their false judgment was what they heard from him (ﷺ), He answered that by showing the exaltedness of his station and the brilliance of his proof, and so it was said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 68, verse 52:

﴿And it is not but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "yaqūlūn" (they say), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is only the waw, or together with the generality of "al-ʿālamīn" (the worlds), as has been said. It serves to show the utter falsehood of their statement, and to astonish the listeners at their audacity in uttering such a monstrous claim. That is: they say this while the reality is that it is a reminder and an exposition, for the worlds, of everything they need in the affairs of their religion. So where is the one to whom it was revealed, who is acquainted with its secrets (ṭurran, entirely) and encompasses all its realities, in contrast to what they have said? It has also been said that its meaning is honour and excellence, based on His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]; and the generality of "al-ʿālamīn" is due to the concern in it for what benefits them. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that he is a reminder and an honour to the worlds, which is beyond doubt. It was preferred on the ground that the sentence, when referred to him, would be explicit in refuting their false claim. But you know that the first is better, and Allah the Exalted knows best.
